2.name: text_block

0.name: block
0.value:
Measures how spread out the values of an array are: the standard deviation, the typical distance of a value from the mean.

Values packed tightly together give a small std; values scattered widely give a large one; values all the same give 0. It is in the same units as the data, so a std of 0.2 on readings in metres means they typically sit about 20 cm either side of their average. Reach for it to tell a steady signal from a jittery one, to measure noise, or to set a threshold in "how many std from the mean".

HOW IT IS WORKED OUT:
Take the mean; take each value's distance from it; square those distances and average them (that average is the variance, np.var); take the square root to get back to the data's units. The average divides by the number of values N - the "population" std. Some tools (a spreadsheet's STDEV, for one) divide by N - 1 instead, which gives a slightly larger answer for small arrays: for 1 2 3 4 np.std gives 1.118, STDEV 1.291.

THE axis MENU:
With no axis (the default) the whole array is reduced to one number. With axis 0 the reduction runs DOWN each column, giving one result per column; with axis 1 it runs ALONG each row, giving one result per row. For a table of 5 frames (rows) of 4 sensors (columns), axis 0 answers "how much did each sensor jitter", axis 1 "how far apart were the sensors at each frame". The axis named is the one that disappears: a 5 by 4 array gives 4 values on axis 0, 5 on axis 1.

SYNTAX:
np.std <axis: int>
With no argument there is no axis: one std for the whole array.

EXAMPLE:
np.std 0

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

in:
The array (a list or a single number is turned into one). Every array that arrives is measured and the result sent - the only inlet that makes the node send.

axis (menu, also an inlet):
Which way to reduce - see THE axis MENU. Changing it does NOT send by itself; the next array uses it. The menu offers None (the whole array) and the axes the last array had (None and 0 for a 1-D array); a message None into the axis inlet also returns to the whole array. An axis the array does not have is treated as its last axis for that array only: the choice is kept, so one 1-D array through np.std 1 does not stop the 2-D arrays that follow from being measured along axis 1.

OUTPUTS:

std:
With no axis, one number, never negative. With an axis, an array one dimension smaller: one std per column (axis 0) or per row (axis 1).

SPREAD AND SHIFT (top demo):
make_noise makes 64 random values, scaled so that at spread 1 and shift 0 their mean is exactly 0 and their std exactly 1; the plot shows them as points. Drag spread: the cloud widens and np.std follows it exactly - spread 2, std 2. Drag shift: the whole cloud moves up or down, np.mean follows it, and np.std does not change at all. The mean says WHERE the values are, the std how SPREAD they are; the two are independent. At spread 0 every value is the same and the std is 0.

ONE STD PER SENSOR (lower demo):
make_jitter makes 16 frames of 4 sensors, each sensor jittering more than the one before (its values times 0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0); click the button for new frames. np.std 0 measures down each column: the strip under the table gives one std per sensor, each under its column, rising from left to right - about 0.06, 0.17, 0.35 and 0.58 (a value spread evenly from -1 to 1 has a std of about 0.58).

RELATED:
np.var is the std squared - same information, squared units. np.mean is the centre the std is measured from. np.robust_mean uses a sturdier measure of spread (the median distance from the median) to reject outliers. np.amax and np.amin give the extremes rather than the typical spread.
